# Data viz - One variable at a time
The different variables are logical, character and double.

Just to use the logical variables as categories, run the following code chunk first!

```{r}
candy_df <- candy_df %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.logical), as_factor))
```

## Exercise 2

Complete the following code to get the data viz to represent "how many candies contain caramel via bar plot". Fill in the blanks, remove the # symbol in front of your code and the execute the code chunk via green play button.

```{r}
ggplot(candy_rankings, aes(x = caramel)) +
geom_bar() +
     labs(title = "Number of Candies that Contain Caramel")
```
In exersise 2 we can see that aroiund 70 candies do not have caramel and around 20 do have caramel.

## Exercise 3

Now look at a numerical variable, such as `winpercent`. Create an histogram for this variable using ggplot2 functions below. Include informative x and y labels and a title, as a good practice.

```{r}
ggplot(candy_df, aes(x = winpercent)) +
  geom_histogram(
    fill = "skyblue",
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Candy Win Percentages",
    x = "Win Percentage",
    y = "Number of Candies"
  )

```
The histogram shows the distribution of candy win percentages. It allows us to identify where most candies are concentrated and whether the distribution is symmetrical or skewed.
```{r}
ggplot(candy_df, aes(x = winpercent)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 20,
    fill = "skyblue",
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Candy Win Percentage (Binwidth = 20)",
    x = "Win Percentage",
    y = "Number of Candies"
  )
```
Increasing the bin width to 20 creates fewer, wider bars. It makes the data overall easier to see but hides the smaller data set.

# Data viz - more than one variable

## Exercise 4

How about using the both variables; chocolate vs winpercent? Run the following incomplete code snippet to get a faceted visualization.

Fill in the blanks, remove the # symbol in front of your code and the execute the code chunk via green play button.

```{r}
ggplot(candy_df, aes(x = winpercent, fill = caramel)) +
 geom_histogram() +
  facet_wrap(~chocolate)+
labs(
    title = "Win Percentage by Chocolate and Caramel",
    x = "Win Percentage",
    y = "Number of Candies"
)
```


- Consider adding the `fill = caramel` within the aes() vs. geom_histogram(), what do you get?
Faceting separates the candies into chocolate and non-chocolate categories. Adding caramel as a fill variable allows us to compare the distribution of win percentages according to both chocolate and caramel content.
